title: Supervise work unit to achieve work unit objectives (individuals and teams)

lessons.title: Setting objectives and planning the work
lessons.html:
The supervisor's job

A supervisor turns the farm or yard's goals into daily work that gets done safely, on time and to standard. On a stud farm or livery yard, your work unit may be a team of grooms; on a mixed farm, it may be the livestock team or a harvesting crew.

From goals to work unit objectives

Start with what management wants, for example: "All mares scanned and foaling records up to date by 30 September" or "Reduce lost workdays from injuries this season." Turn each into SMART objectives:

  • Specific: clear about what must be done.
  • Measurable: you can count or check it.
  • Achievable: possible with the people, time and tools you have.
  • Relevant: linked to the business goal.
  • Time-bound: has a deadline.

Planning the work

  1. Break objectives into tasks: for example, feeding, mucking out, turnout, exercise, health checks and record keeping.
  2. Estimate time and resources: people, vehicles, feed, tack, tools and budget.
  3. Allocate tasks: match tasks to skills and experience. Pair new workers with experienced ones.
  4. Draw up a duty roster: include weekends, leave and rest days in line with the Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997 and the sectoral determination for farm workers.
  5. Plan for safety: identify hazards (kicks, machinery, chemicals, heat) and controls, as required by the OHS Act 85 of 1993.
  6. Plan for problems: what if a worker is absent, a vehicle breaks down or a horse is sick?

Communicating the plan

Hold a short meeting at the start of each day or week. Explain the objectives, who does what and the safety points. Check understanding by asking questions, and give the team a chance to raise concerns. Put the roster on a notice board in the tack room or office.

lessons.title: Leading individuals and teams
lessons.html:
Building an effective team

People work best when they know what is expected, have the tools to do it, and feel respected. As supervisor you:

  • Treat everyone fairly and consistently, regardless of language, culture or gender.
  • Explain the reason for tasks, not only the instruction.
  • Recognise good work, in public where appropriate.
  • Deal with conflict early and privately.
  • Support training and skills development.

Delegating

  1. Choose the right person.
  2. Explain the task, standard and deadline clearly.
  3. Give the authority and resources needed.
  4. Agree check-in points.
  5. Stay accountable: you delegate the task, not the responsibility.

Motivating

Motivation comes from fair pay and conditions, but also from respect, clear goals, involvement in decisions, learning opportunities and seeing the results of one's work. A groom who is told that the mare he prepared produced a healthy foal feels part of the success.

Handling poor performance

  • Find the cause first: lack of skill, unclear instructions, personal problems or attitude.
  • Talk privately, describe the behaviour and its effect, and agree on actions.
  • Offer training or support where the problem is skill.
  • Follow the company's disciplinary code and the Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995 for misconduct. Keep written records.

Team meetings

Keep them short, regular and focused: progress, problems, safety and next steps. Encourage quieter members to speak.

lessons.title: Monitoring, reporting and improving
lessons.html:
Monitoring performance

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Monitor against the objectives you set:

ObjectiveMeasureHow to check
Horses fed on timeFeed times metFeed chart signed off
Stables cleanDaily inspection scoreWalk-through checklist
Health checks doneDaily health sheet completeReview sheets each afternoon
SafetyIncidents and near missesIncident register
CostsFeed and bedding useStock records vs budget

Giving feedback

  • Give it soon after the event, be specific and focus on the work, not the person.
  • Balance positive and corrective feedback.
  • Agree on what will be done differently and follow up.

Reporting to management

Report progress regularly in writing: objectives achieved, problems, causes, actions taken and support needed. Bring solutions, not only problems.

Continuous improvement

After each season or project, review with the team: What went well? What went wrong? What will we change? Update procedures and training plans. Small, steady improvements, such as a better feed room layout or a clearer roster, add up.

Key points

  • Turn business goals into SMART work unit objectives.
  • Plan tasks, resources, rosters and safety, and communicate clearly.
  • Delegate tasks but keep the responsibility.
  • Address poor performance by finding the cause and following the disciplinary code.
  • Monitor with simple measures and give specific feedback.
  • Review and improve after each season.
